content.passage: Health experts regularly recommend that teenagers do at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-hard physical activity every day. This doesn’t necessarily mean competitive sport. Activities such as cycling to school, swimming, or even a brisk walk, all count towards the daily target. What makes exercise particularly powerful is its effect on the brain: physical activity causes the release of endorphins, chemicals that reduce feelings of stress and anxiety at the same time as boosting mood and self-confidence. Furthermore, teenagers who exercise regularly tend to sleep more deeply and report higher levels of concentration during school hours. Despite these well-documented benefits, a landmark WHO-led study found that more than 80% of teenagers worldwide fail to meet the recommended daily activity levels, largely due to sedentary screen-based habits.

content.script: Host: Welcome to today's student broadcast on modern stress and mental health. Today we discuss findings from a recent Egyptian school health survey involving 450 students aged 14 to 17. The data revealed that over 65 percent of respondents experienced elevated stress levels during major examination periods. Interestingly, students who engaged in at least thirty minutes of daily physical activity reported noticeably lower anxiety levels, even when controlling for academic workload. Furthermore, the report highlighted distinct coping mechanisms between urban and rural cohorts, emphasizing the necessity of accessible school-based counseling services.

content.question: Why do academic writers use hedging language such as 'suggests', 'may', or 'could'?

To make their sentences as dramatic as possible.
To confuse the reader about basic statistical facts.
To eliminate all grammar rules from the text.
content.correctAnswer: To present claims with appropriate caution and objective distance.
content.reason: Hedging allows researchers to state findings cautiously without over-generalizing.
